title: Operator-signed Change Assertion Protocol (PRD - WIP)
content:
Purpose
---
This doc proposes an "operator-signed change assertion" protocol for Private deployments. Goal: provide a lightweight, cryptographically-rooted assertion attached to every customer-managed network change so Redwood and the customer can reconstruct intent, authorization and runtime state for post-mortem, audit, and automated gating.

Background / problem statement
- Private customers run operator-controlled network components (firewalls, peering, NAT, on-prem adaptors). When control-plane changes occur (routing, DNS rewrites, peering updates), we need high-confidence audit records that tie the change to an authorized human/agent and to the exact pre/post network snapshot.
- Current logs: control-plane events + operator activity logs + sampled telemetry. These are useful but frequently lack: (a) tamper-resistant assertion from the customer operator, (b) a compact change token that ties multi-source events, (c) a deterministic pre-change simulation result for safety gates.
- Without improved assertions, rollbacks and incident forensic work are slow and error-prone, increasing MTTR and raising compliance risk.

High-level proposal
- When an operator initiates a network change, the customer operator signs a structured assertion (Change Assertion) with a key the customer controls (KMS/HSM or customer-supplied cert). Redwood control plane returns a change-token that is anchored in our audit log and correlates: assertion, simulated impact snapshot, requested resources, and operator identity.
- Change Assertion components (minimal): change-id, timestamp, actor-id, operator-signature, change-diff (high level), nonce/challenge, optional pre-sim-hash, intended rollout policy.
- Workflow: 1) prepare -> 2) simulate (sandbox) -> 3) assert (operator signs) -> 4) submit -> 5) gate evaluation -> 6) apply + stream enriched audit events -> 7) finalization + retention.

Goals / success criteria
- Security: assertion must be verifiable using customer-managed credentials; Redwood must be able to verify but not be able to forge.
- Forensics: given token + logs + snapshots we can reconstruct timeline and exact decision inputs in >= 95% of sampled changes.
- Ops: reduce manual triage effort on network incidents by 30% in pilot customers.
- Compliance: enable attestation artifacts that satisfy SOC2 / ISO-style auditors for change evidence.

Non-goals
- Not intended to replace full packet-level capture or long-term SIEM retention.
- Not a replacement for policy engines (we keep existing approval policies; this provides stronger evidence and better gating inputs).

Detailed design
1) Operator identity and key models (support multiple):
   - Customer KMS (recommended): customer provides public key/cert to Redwood during onboarding and rotates per their policy.
   - Customer HSM-backed signing service: Redwood sends a challenge to customer endpoint; the endpoint returns signed assertion (mutual-TLS).
   - Redwood-managed ephemeral keys (fallback for quick-start): keys created per-tenant with auto-rotate; customer consents but for highest assurance customers use their own KMS.

2) Assertion format (textual, JSON-compatible, but canonicalized):
   - fields: change_id, issued_at, actor_id, actor_role, change_summary, diff_hash, pre_sim_snapshot_hash, rollout_plan_id, challenge_nonce, signature_algo, signature_b64, key_id, signature_metadata
   - canonical form: newline-delimited key=val sorted to avoid ambiguous signing.

3) Simulation step (required for gated classes):
   - Redwood runs sandbox simulation against an isolated topology mirror and produces a deterministic snapshot (pre and post simulated state digests).
   - Simulation includes reachability matrix, firewall rule evaluation, routing table diffs, and high-level latency/cost delta estimates.
   - Simulation output is hashed and included in the assertion (pre_sim_snapshot_hash).

4) Gate evaluation engine inputs
   - Mandatory inputs: assertion (verifiable), change diff metadata, simulation digest, policy rules, capacity/latency SLO heuristics, historical failure rates.
   - Gate outcomes: approve, require-manual-review, reject. Each outcome emits an enriched audit event containing the change-token, gate-decision, reasoning, and correlation ids.

5) Audit log enrichment and retention
   - Every enriched event: change-token, assertion (or assertion reference), simulation-digest, gate-result, operator-id, control-plane request id, affected-resources list.
   - Immutable append-only ledger: Redwood stores the enriched event with a server-side signature and incremental sequence id.
   - Retention: default 90 days in hot store; 7 years archive available under add-on for enterprise (compliance).

6) Forensic reconstruction pattern
   - Given change-token, collect: assertion (or key reference), sequence of enriched events, telemetry snippets (sampled pcap/flow where available), simulation snapshots.
   - Automated reconstruction tool will: verify operator signature, validate simulation hash, replay state diffs in an offline sandbox, and produce a reproducible timeline doc (PDF/JSON) for auditors.

Operational considerations / edge cases
- Clock skew: assertions include issued_at and we accept +/- 5m by default; for stricter customers support NTP-signed timestamps via external signer.
- Missing customer key: provide one-time override flow with elevated manual review and extra telemetry capture; all overrides produce a distinct override assertion and are fully flagged in logs.
- Replay resistance: include nonce/challenge bound to current request id to prevent replaying old signed assertions.
- Partial sign flows: multi-operator approval (support threshold signatures or multiple assertions aggregated into a single change-token).

Security / threat model notes
- Threats: stolen operator keys, forged assertions, tampering with simulation snapshot, rollback attacks on audit store.
- Mitigations: require key-id and public-key binding at onboarding; per-assertion server-side signature; immutable ledger with sequence ids and cross-checksums; optional customer-driven HSM signing.

Integration with customer-managed networking
- Onboarding: API to register public key/cert, registers allowed signer identities and optional key rotation windows.
- Runtime: Redwood control plane verifies assertion against registered key id and validates simulation-digest before gate evaluation.
- Customer tooling: provide a small CLI utility that generates canonical assertions (useful for customers who want to sign locally before submitting change requests).

Observability / metrics
- Key metrics to track in Console: assertion-verification-rate, gate-decision-distribution, simulation-failure-rate, % changes with operator-signed assertion, average time between assert->apply, override-count.
- Dashboards / alerting: alert when verification failures > X% or manual overrides spike.

Backward compatibility and migration
- Existing customers: continue to use current change flow; provide opt-in toggle for operator-signed assertions.
- Migration plan: pilot with 3 customers, collect feedback, iterate on assertion schema and CLI.

UX notes (developer/operator-facing)
- When editing a change in Console: show simulation results inline and a "Sign & Submit" button (trigger local signing or redirect to customer HSM signer endpoint).
- CLI: redwoodctl network simulate -> redwoodctl network sign-assertion --key-id ... -> redwoodctl network apply --assertion-file ...

Open questions / decisions needed
- Default retention policy for assertions vs. enriched events (legal to decide).
- Multi-signature support: native threshold signing vs. aggregate assertions.
- Whether Redwood should offer an off-the-shelf HSM signing gateway for customers without KMS.

Next steps / action items
- Engineering: prototype verification flow + immutable append-only storage schema (owner: Ravi).
- Applied ML / Observability: design simulation snapshot digest and deterministic sandbox (owner: Lena).
- Solutions Eng: recruit 3 pilot customers and draft onboarding checklist (owner: Marcus).
- Security: threat model review and KMS integration spec (owner: Sofia).
- Timeline: 8-week prototype, 12-week pilot.

Notes to self / loose ideas
- Consider adding short-lived signed "change tickets" that embed sprint/context for auditors.
- Could tie assertions into rollout canaries so canary events automatically reference the original change-token.
- We might also include a privacy-preserving digest for simulated packet traces instead of full capture for customers concerned about PII.

References / links
- See linked artifacts above for relevant Jira tickets and Slack threads.
- Example canonical signing library: reference impl in github:infra/automation#312 (prototype).
